query_text: Should corporations be required to pay taxes on all profits?

messages.content: Should corporations be required to pay taxes on all profits?

message.content:
Whether corporations **should** be required to pay taxes on all profits is a policy question, not a fact question; under current U.S. law, many corporations already pay tax on profits, but not always at the full statutory rate and not all business entities are taxed at the corporate level.[1][3][4]

If the goal is **broad tax base and fairness**, requiring tax on all profits would reduce the ability to use deductions, credits, loss carryforwards, and pass-through structures to eliminate tax in profitable years.[1][2][6] Supporters argue this would make the system more consistent because the corporate income tax currently has a 21% statutory rate, yet some profitable firms pay little or nothing due to tax preferences and planning.[1][5][6]

If the goal is **investment and economic efficiency**, opponents argue that taxing all profits can increase the cost of capital and reinforce the “double tax” on C-corporation earnings, since profits can be taxed once at the corporate level and again when distributed as dividends.[1][3] They also note that many small and medium businesses are not taxed as separate corporations at all, because pass-through entities report income on owners’ returns instead.[1][4][8]

A practical middle ground is usually a **minimum tax on profitable corporations**, rather than a pure “tax every dollar of profit at the full rate” rule.[5][6] That approach preserves the corporate tax while limiting cases where large profitable firms pay little or nothing in a given year.[5][6]

If you want, I can also lay out the **main arguments for and against** this policy in a simple debate format.
